name: Api Etoile

origin.parentage: Unknown; a member of the Api (Lady apple) group

history: A very old curiosity of the Api family, first described by the Swiss botanist Jean Bauhin (d. 1613) as a 'pentagonal apple'. It later spread to Italy and to Paris, and was rediscovered in Switzerland in 1981; it survives mainly in specialist collections.

look.description: Small, flattened fruit with five pronounced bumps that make a star outline seen from the end; pale green skin with a pink cheek and a waxy coating.

taste.summary: Firm, yellowish-white flesh. One grower source rates the flavour highly, aromatic with a sweet fruitiness and enough acid, while a German source says it looks better than it tastes; it is grown mainly for its novel shape.
taste.best_eaten: Winter, after some weeks in store

tree.notes: Described as having long, slender branches. Little reliable growing data is published.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; plant with a mid-season diploid to be safe.

climate.best_climates: Central European conditions like its Swiss home; a very late variety that needs a long season to finish.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; as a late Alpine-region apple it is unlikely to suit low-chill or short-season areas.

health.other: No disease data found. The waxy skin is said to help the fruit keep.

grow_notes: A collector's apple grown for its star shape. Give it a warm, sheltered position so the late fruit ripens, and plant a mid-season pollinator nearby.

name: Ard Cairn Russet
history: Found around 1890 by the Cork nurseryman Baylor Hartland and named after his Ard Cairn nursery. It won an RHS Award of Merit in 1910 and is one of the better-known Irish heritage apples.

look.description: Medium, flat-topped conical fruit, heavily coated in russet over a yellow ground, with some red streaks showing through.

taste.summary: Dense, firm flesh that is sweet but low in acid and rather dry; the aroma is slight. Orange Pippin likens the flavour to banana. It is said to be at its best after a few months in store.

tree.notes: Fairly vigorous; branches tend to form very narrow crotch angles, so train them out early. One grower reports light crops on a vigorous rootstock.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection flowering dates put it mid-season (group 3); Orange Pippin lists group 4. Plant with a group 3-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates like southern Ireland and western Britain; reported to tolerate most temperate regions.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; very hot or very cold continental climates are untested.

health.other: Described as having fairly good all-round disease resistance.

grow_notes: A useful russet for wetter western sites. Train young branches to wider angles, and store the fruit for a while before eating; it also makes a good juice.

name: Aurora Golden Gala

origin.place: Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre, Summerland, British Columbia, Canada
origin.raised_by: Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre (Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada)

history: A yellow dessert apple from the Summerland breeding programme in British Columbia, tested as 8S6923 and named in 2003. It is marketed mainly in Canada and the US, where it has done well in taste panels.

look.description: Medium, slightly tall fruit with thin, glossy, clear yellow skin.

taste.summary: Very crisp, breaking, juicy flesh with a sweet, well-balanced flavour and some aroma. It keeps its firmness for months in store.

tree.notes: Little published tree data outside commercial trials.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not found; Gala and Splendour are both mid-season, so a mid-season partner is a reasonable choice.

climate.best_climates: Sunny inland fruit valleys with warm days and cold winters, like the Okanagan where it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in cool, wet maritime climates or very hot lowlands.

grow_notes: A modern commercial yellow apple best suited to sunny, dry fruit regions. It can be picked quite ripe and still stores well.

name: Bailey

origin.place: Perry, Wyoming County, New York, USA

history: A nineteenth-century 'sweet' apple from Perry in western New York, grown from about 1840. It was valued as a sweet table apple but was never a strong keeper.

look.description: Medium to large, roundish or slightly conical fruit, bright yellow mostly covered by deep red, with pale flecks.

taste.summary: Firm, yellow-tinged, moderately juicy flesh that is distinctly sweet with very little acid. Growers say the sweetness is fullest after the first frosts.

tree.notes: Productive, but unsprayed trees give much poor-grade, scabby or knotty fruit.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter north-eastern US conditions like western New York.
climate.poor_climates: Humid areas where scab pressure is high produce blemished, misshapen fruit.

health.other: Prone to apple scab; fruit can be scabby and knotty without spraying.

grow_notes: Grow it for its old-fashioned sweet flavour in a cold-winter area, in an open, airy spot to limit scab. Eat the fruit within a couple of months.

name: Bancroft

origin.place: Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada
origin.raised_by: Division of Horticulture, Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa

history: Selected at Ottawa in 1930 and released around 1935 as a late-keeping McIntosh-type apple for Canadian growers. It was once grown commercially in Ontario but is now mostly a heritage variety.

look.description: Medium, slightly flattened fruit almost covered in dark red flush and stripes over greenish yellow, with some dotted russet.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, juicy, greenish-white flesh with a mild subacid, refreshingly fruity flavour, finer in texture than McIntosh. It holds flavour and texture well into spring, though it softens in long storage.

tree.notes: A tough, dependable tree that starts bearing young; spreading to drooping habit.

pollination.notes: Flowers early at Brogdale (about group 2); needs a pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates like eastern Ontario, where it was bred for hardiness and long keeping.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to give soft, poorly coloured fruit, as with other McIntosh types.

grow_notes: A hardy keeper for cold areas. Plant with an early-flowering pollinator, pick in mid-October and store cool for eating after Christmas.

name: Baumann's Reinette
history: Thought to come from the Belgian pomologist Van Mons and dedicated to the Baumann brothers' nursery at Bollwiller in Alsace; it was recorded in 1811. It became a classic Christmas apple in Germany and gained an RHS First Class Certificate in 1878.

look.description: Medium, flattish fruit almost covered in brilliant crimson flush and stripes; several colour forms exist.

taste.summary: Rather coarse, fairly juicy, slightly chewy flesh with a sweet-sharp but plain flavour and only a faint aroma. It looks better than it tastes and cannot match the aromatic reinettes.

tree.notes: Fairly small tree that crops early, heavily and regularly. Wood is vulnerable to hard frost.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering; regarded as a good pollinator. Blossom fairly frost-hardy but can be caught by late frosts.

climate.best_climates: Sunny, moderately elevated central European sites with even moisture and rich soil.
climate.poor_climates: Frost hollows and wet, scab-prone sites.

health.other: Susceptible to scab, canker, aphids, wood frost, lenticel spotting, skin russeting and storage rots; resists shrivelling in store.

grow_notes: A reliable, decorative cropper for a sunny site with good soil. Avoid frost pockets and damp, scab-prone spots; store the fruit cool for winter use.

name: Baxter's Pearmain
history: A Norfolk apple introduced by George Lindley in 1821 and grown as a dual-purpose orchard variety in East Anglia.

look.description: Medium, oblong pearmain-shaped fruit; colour details not confirmed.

taste.summary: Pale, somewhat coarse and rather dry flesh with a slightly acid flavour that the National Fruit Collection compares to Blenheim Orange.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly late-mid season at Brogdale (about group 4).

climate.best_climates: Drier eastern English conditions like its Norfolk home.

grow_notes: A local East Anglian apple for heritage collections. Pick in mid-October and store for winter use, fresh or cooked.

name: Beeley Pippin
history: Raised around 1880 by the Reverend C. Sculthorpe at Beeley in Derbyshire and taken into the National Fruit Collection in 1916. It remains little known outside collections.

look.description: Medium to large, broadly conical fruit, greenish yellow with an orange-red flush over a quarter to half of the skin.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, slightly tough flesh, juicy and sweet with a pleasant aromatic flavour and moderate acidity. An early apple best eaten soon after picking.

tree.notes: Average vigour with a spreading habit.

pollination.notes: Early flowering: Brogdale dates suggest group 2 and Orange Pippin lists group 1. Pair with another early-flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool English conditions, including the Derbyshire uplands where it arose.
climate.poor_climates: Early blossom is exposed to spring frosts in cold hollows.

grow_notes: An early dessert apple for northern or upland English gardens. Because it blossoms early, avoid frost pockets and plant an early-flowering partner.
